title: Navigate Between Files with Jumps
summary: Chapter 9 (Tips 56–59) explains jump-based navigation: jumps record cursor positions in a per-window jump list that <C-o> and <C-i> traverse backward and forward, and unlike ordinary motions they can cross file boundaries. It contrasts the jump list with the per-buffer change list (g; and g,) and the `. and `^ marks, then shows how gf treats a filepath under the cursor as a hyperlink configured by 'suffixesadd' and 'path'. The chapter closes with global marks (m{letter}), which persist across files and sessions and are worth setting before commands such as :vimgrep.

commands.meaning: Jump backward through the jump list, like a browser's back button
commands.evidence: In web browsers, we’re used to using the back button to return to pages that we visited earlier. Vim provides a similar feature by way of the jump list: the <C-o> command is like the back button, while the complementary <C-i> command is like the forward button. These commands allow us to traverse Vim’s jump list, but what exactly is a jump?

As a memory aid for g; and g,, it may help to remember that the ; and , commands can be used to repeat or reverse the f{char} command (see Tip 50).

commands.meaning: Restore the cursor to the last insertion point and switch back to Insert mode
commands.evidence: The `^ mark references the last insertion, which is slightly more specific than the last change. If we leave Insert mode and then scroll around the document, we can quickly carry on where we left off by pressing gi (giⓘ). In a single move, that uses the `^ mark to restore the cursor position and then switches back into Insert mode. It’s a great little time saver!

commands.meaning: Create a mark at the cursor; uppercase letters create global marks
commands.evidence: The m{letter} command allows us to create a mark at the current cursor position (mⓘ). Lowercase letters create marks that are local to a buffer, whereas uppercase letters create global marks. Having set a mark, we can snap our cursor back to it with the `{letter} command (`ⓘ).

concepts.name: Jump list
concepts.evidence: In web browsers, we’re used to using the back button to return to pages that we visited earlier. Vim provides a similar feature by way of the jump list: the <C-o> command is like the back button, while the complementary <C-i> command is like the forward button. These commands allow us to traverse Vim’s jump list, but what exactly is a jump?

concepts.name: Jumps vs. motions

concepts.name: Mapping <Tab> also overrides <C-i>
concepts.evidence: Beware that if you attempt to create a mapping for the <Tab> key, it will also be triggered when you press <C-i> (and vice versa). That may not seem like a problem, but consider this: if you map the <Tab> key to something else, it will overwrite the default behavior of the <C-i> command. Think carefully about whether that’s a worthwhile trade-off. The jump list is much less useful if you can only traverse it in one direction.

concepts.name: Last-change marks (`. and `^)
concepts.evidence: Vim automatically creates a couple of marks that complement the change list. The `. mark always references the position of the last change (`.ⓘ), while the `^ mark tracks the position of the cursor the last time that Insert mode was stopped (`^ⓘ).

concepts.name: Change list per buffer vs. jump list per window
concepts.evidence: Vim maintains a change list for each individual buffer in an editing session. By contrast, a separate jump list is created for each window.

concepts.name: Filepath under the cursor as a hyperlink
concepts.evidence: Vim treats filenames in our document as a kind of hyperlink. When configured properly, we can use the gf command to go to the filename under the cursor.

concepts.name: 'suffixesadd' extension lookup
concepts.evidence: The ‘suffixesadd’ option allows us to specify one or more file extensions, which Vim will attempt to use when looking up a filename with the gf command ('suffixesadd'ⓘ). We can set it up by running this command:

concepts.name: 'path' search directories
concepts.evidence: That’s where the ‘path’ option comes in ('path'ⓘ). We can configure this to reference a comma-separated list of directories. When we use the gf command, Vim checks each of the directories listed in ‘path’ to see if it contains a filename that matches the text under the cursor. The ‘path’ setting is also used by the :find command, which we covered in Tip 43.

concepts.name: Global marks
concepts.evidence: A global mark is a kind of bookmark that allows us to jump between files. Marks can be especially useful for snapping back to a file after exploring a codebase.

concepts.name: Global marks persist between sessions
concepts.evidence: Try this: open up your vimrc file and press mV to set a global mark (mnemonic: V for vimrc). Switch to another file and then press `V, and you should snap back to the global mark you set in the vimrc file. By default, global marks are persisted between editing sessions (although this behavior can be configured; see 'viminfo'ⓘ). Now you can always open up your vimrc file with two keystrokes—that is, unless you set the global V mark to another location.
